title: Hungry in the woods
def: If you are hungry in the woods, eat the food you carried and focus first on water, shelter, warmth, and being found, because a person can go weeks without food but only days without water.
look: a hunger that feels urgent but is not an emergency
packed food, even small amounts
water, warmth, and signals come first
use: Eat what you carried in small amounts, keep warm and hydrated, and stop to make a plan. Save energy and signal for help. Fish or known foods only if you know how.
not: Do not start by eating wild plants or mushrooms; mistakes can be deadly.
call: Call 911 or use satellite SOS if you are lost or hurt.

title: Danger zone: 40 to 140 F
also: how long can food sit out
def: The danger zone is 40 to 140 F (4 to 60 C), where bacteria multiply fast, so perishable food should not stay out more than two hours, or one hour above 90 F.
look: perishable food left out on a counter or picnic table
food not kept cold in a cooler
hot food that cooled slowly
use: Keep cold food at or below 40 F and hot food at or above 140 F. Put leftovers in the fridge or cooler within two hours (one hour if it is above 90 F). Use ice packs and a thermometer in the cooler.
not: Do not leave perishable food out for more than two hours, and do not taste it to see whether it is safe.

title: Safe minimum cooking temperatures
def: Use a food thermometer: 165 F (74 C) for poultry and leftovers, 160 F (71 C) for ground meats and egg dishes, and 145 F (63 C) for whole cuts of meat and fish with a three-minute rest.
look: poultry and reheated food: 165 F
ground beef, pork, and ground game: 160 F
whole beef, pork, lamb, venison, and fish: 145 F
use: Insert the thermometer into the thickest part, away from bone, and let the temperature settle. Do not rely on color.
not: Do not judge doneness by color or juice; ground meat can be brown before it is safe.

title: Are leftovers, picnic food, or cooler food still safe?
def: Leftovers are safe for three to four days in the fridge and picnic or cooler food is safe only if it stayed at 40 F or below; when in doubt, throw it out.
look: how long it sat in the danger zone
a cooler with ice still present and food cold
smell is not a reliable test
use: Reheat leftovers to 165 F, keep coolers full of ice or ice packs, and discard perishable food that was out over two hours (one hour above 90 F).
not: Do not rely on smell or taste; harmful bacteria often do not change them.

title: Food hygiene in the field
def: Wash hands and tools, keep raw meat separate from ready-to-eat food, and cook to a safe temperature.
look: hands washed with soap or sanitizer
separate cutting boards and knives
cooler kept cold
use: Wash hands with soap and treated water before touching food, bag raw meat separately, wash utensils, and keep the cooler in shade.
not: Do not reuse a plate or knife that touched raw meat without washing.

title: Food in the fridge and freezer during an outage
also: how long does a fridge stay cold
def: A closed refrigerator keeps food safe about 4 hours without power; a full freezer holds for about 48 hours (24 if half full) if the door stays shut.
look: a thermometer in the fridge at 40 F or below
ice crystals still in the freezer food
a cooler with ice for backup
use: Keep doors closed, group food together, use ice or dry ice carefully, and check temperatures. Discard perishable food above 40 F for more than two hours.
not: Do not taste food to test it, and do not refreeze food that fully thawed.

title: Making jerky safely
def: Safe jerky starts with heating the meat to a safe internal temperature before or during drying, and the drying alone does not kill bacteria.
look: lean meat sliced thin
heat to 160 F (71 C), poultry to 165 F, then dry at 130 to 140 F (54 to 60 C)
a dry, leathery finish that bends but does not break
use: Follow USDA guidance: marinate in the fridge, steam or oven-heat to the right internal temperature, then dry. Store in a cool dry place.
not: Do not rely on drying alone or dry at too low a temperature.

title: Home canning: pressure canner for meat and vegetables
def: Low-acid foods such as meat and vegetables must be canned in a pressure canner following the USDA guide, because boiling-water canning cannot make them safe from botulism.
look: a pressure canner with a tested gauge
a bulging lid, spurting liquid, or a bad smell
USDA tested processing times
use: Follow the USDA Complete Guide to Home Canning for your food, jar size, and altitude. Check each jar seal before storage.
not: Do not taste food from a jar that bulges, leaks, or smells off; throw it away carefully.
call: Call 911 for double vision, drooping eyelids, or trouble swallowing or breathing after eating home-canned food.

title: Allergies to wild or familiar foods
def: Food allergies can cause hives, swelling, or trouble breathing within minutes; carry any prescribed epinephrine and tell your group.
look: hives, swelling of the lips or tongue, wheezing
vomiting or dizziness after eating
exposure to a known allergen
use: Know your allergens, tell your group, carry medicine, and avoid new wild foods. Use epinephrine as prescribed and call 911.
not: Do not try a wild food if you have a known allergy.
call: Call 911 for any signs of a severe reaction.

title: Cleaning fish and spoilage signs
def: Gut and chill fish quickly; cook it to 145 F; spoiled fish smells sour, feels slimy, and has cloudy eyes.
look: fresh: clear eyes, firm flesh, mild smell
spoiled: sour smell, slime, sunken or cloudy eyes
check state fish consumption advisories
use: Gut the fish soon after catching, keep it on ice, wash your hands, and cook it to 145 F. Check the state health department's fish advisories for mercury and other contaminants.
not: Do not eat fish that smells off, and do not leave it in the sun.
region: Maine and Rhode Island post fish consumption advisories; check them before you eat what you catch.

title: Shellfish closures and red tide
def: Shellfish can carry toxins from algal blooms, and cooking does not remove them, so follow the official closure notices.
look: a posted closure or red tide notice
numbness around the mouth after eating shellfish
state marine resources pages
use: Check the state shellfish closure page before you harvest; if you cannot confirm that the area is open, do not eat shellfish from it.
not: Do not rely on cooking or on the look of the water.
region: Maine DMR and Rhode Island DEM post closure notices; link, never guess.
call: Call 911 for numbness, weakness, or trouble breathing after eating shellfish.
